title: "Workflow Overview"

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(PKNCA)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter, dplyr::select, .quiet = TRUE)
```

## The five-step workflow

Every PKNCA analysis follows the same five steps regardless of route or complexity.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    S1["① Prepare data<br/>concentration data frame<br/>dose data frame"] --> S2
    S2["② PKNCAconc()<br/>define conc column, time column,<br/>grouping variables, optional args (duration, volume)"] --> S3
    S3["③ PKNCAdose()<br/>define dose, time, route<br/>(intravascular / extravascular)"] --> S4
    S4["④ PKNCAdata()<br/>combine conc + dose<br/>specify intervals + imputation + units"] --> S5
    S5["⑤ pk.nca()<br/>run all calculations"] --> S6
    S6["PKNCAresults<br/>summary() / as.data.frame()"]

    style S1 fill:#f0f4ff
    style S6 fill:#e8f5e9
```

## Step-by-step: minimal example

Below is the complete workflow with the built-in `Theoph` dataset (oral theophylline, 12 subjects). The package vignette [Computing NCA Parameters for Theophylline](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v02-example-theophylline.html) works through the same dataset.

### Step 1 — Prepare your data

PKNCA typically takes two separate data frames: one for concentrations and one for doses (dose data are optional, but required for dose-dependent parameters such as CL and Vz). Both must be in **long format** (one row per observation).

```{r}
# Built-in oral theophylline dataset
head(Theoph)
```

The columns are: `Subject`, `Wt` (weight, kg), `Dose` (mg/kg), `Time` (h), `conc` (mg/L).

```{r}
# Concentration data: keep what we need
d_conc <- Theoph |>
  select(Subject, Time, conc)

# Dose data: one row per subject (single dose at time 0)
d_dose <- Theoph |>
  group_by(Subject) |>
  summarise(Dose = Dose[1] * Wt[1], .groups = "drop") |>  # convert mg/kg to mg
  mutate(Time = 0)

head(d_dose)
```

### Step 2 — PKNCAconc

`PKNCAconc` tells PKNCA the structure of your concentration data via a formula:
`concentration ~ time | group1 / group2 / ...`

```{r}
o_conc <- PKNCAconc(d_conc, conc ~ Time | Subject)
print(o_conc)
```

### Step 3 — PKNCAdose

`PKNCAdose` describes the dosing. The `route` argument is critical — it determines which parameters are estimable.

```{r}
o_dose <- PKNCAdose(d_dose, Dose ~ Time | Subject, route = "extravascular")
print(o_dose)
```

### Step 4 — PKNCAdata

`PKNCAdata` combines concentration and dose objects. If you don't specify `intervals`, PKNCA generates them from the dose times. It finds each group's dosing regimen and, for each interval it places, asks `pknca_interval_table()` for the parameters and the imputation that suit that interval's context (≥ 0.13.0). A single dose, as here, gets one interval from the dose to infinity that requests `auclast`, `cmax`, `tmax`, `tlag`, `count_conc`, `half.life`, `aucinf.obs`, `aucpext.obs`, and `cl.obs`. Its `impute` column holds `start_predose_conc0`: a concentration measured at the dose time is kept, a predose concentration is carried forward to the dose time when there is none, and 0 is imputed when there is neither (see the [Concentration Imputation chapter](imputation.qmd)). Multiple-dose data get one row per sampled dosing interval instead (typically the first one and the last one), built on the `aucint.*` family with `start_cmin` or `start_predose` imputation; [Automatic Intervals and Dosing Regimens](auto-intervals.qmd) explains how the regimen is detected and which intervals each design gets.

```{r}
o_data <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose)
```

You can inspect the auto-generated intervals. The interval table has one logical column per known parameter, so this keeps only the columns that request something:

```{r}
o_data$intervals |>
  select(where(~ !is.logical(.x) || any(.x))) |>
  head(3)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Changed in 0.13.0
Before 0.13.0, a single dose got the intervals in the `single.dose.aucs` option instead: `auclast` over 0 to 24 (which assumed hours) plus `cmax`, `tmax`, `half.life`, and `aucinf.obs` over 0 to infinity, with no imputation. Because the single-dose interval now imputes a concentration at the dose time, results change when no sample was taken at the dose time: AUCs that need a concentration there are now calculated from the imputed one, where the legacy intervals give `NA` with an exclusion reason (see the [Concentration Imputation chapter](imputation.qmd)). `PKNCA.options(auto.interval.method = "legacy")` (or `options = list(auto.interval.method = "legacy")` in `PKNCAdata()`) restores the previous parameter lists. The [Interval Selection chapter](intervals.qmd) shows how to build the same tables yourself with `pknca_interval_table()`.
:::

### Step 5 — pk.nca

Run all calculations:

```{r}
o_nca <- pk.nca(o_data)
```

### Results

```{r}
# Tidy data frame of all computed parameters
as.data.frame(o_nca) |> head(20)
```

```{r}
# Summary table (geometric mean and geometric CV% by default for most parameters)
summary(o_nca)
```

## Specifying intervals manually

Automatic intervals cover the common designs. When you need other windows or parameters, define intervals yourself, either as a data frame as below or with the helpers `pknca_interval_table()` and `interval_add_param()` described in the [Interval Selection chapter](intervals.qmd).

An **interval** is a row in a data frame with:

- `start`, `end`: time boundaries
- One column per parameter set to `TRUE` to request that parameter

```{r}
# Request specific parameters over a specific window
my_intervals <- data.frame(
  start  = 0,
  end    = Inf,
  auclast  = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs = TRUE,
  cmax   = TRUE,
  tmax   = TRUE,
  half.life = TRUE
)

o_data2 <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = my_intervals)
o_nca2  <- pk.nca(o_data2)
as.data.frame(o_nca2)
```

## Controlling calculations with PKNCA.options()

`PKNCA.options()` is the global settings registry. Call it with no arguments to get a named list of all current settings. See also the vignette [Options for Controlling PKNCA](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v40-options-for-controlling-PKNCA.html).

```{r}
current_options <- PKNCA.options()
names(current_options)
```

PKNCA `r packageVersion("PKNCA")` has `r length(PKNCA.options())` options. (Printing `PKNCA.options()` itself shows every value, including `single.dose.aucs`, which is a full interval data frame with one column per parameter.) Two helpers read the registry without changing it (≥ 0.13.0 for `PKNCA_options_defaults()`): `PKNCA_options_defaults()` gives the default of one option or all of them, which is useful after the current values have been changed, and `PKNCA.options.describe()` gives the package's own description of an option.

```{r}
PKNCA_options_defaults("auto.interval.tolerance")
PKNCA.options.describe("auto.interval.tolerance")
```

All options and what they control:

**AUC / integration**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `auc.method` | `"lin up/log down"` | Integration rule: `"lin up/log down"`, `"linear"`, or `"lin-log"` |

Each rule is derived in [AUC integration methods](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v23-auc-integration-methods.html).

**Half-life / λz**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `min.hl.points` | `3` | Minimum data points for a valid λz regression |
| `max.hl.points` | `Inf` | Maximum number of points that automatic point selection may use; must be more than `min.hl.points` (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `min.hl.start.time` | `0` | Earliest time at which automatic point selection may start the λz regression; `0` does not restrict it (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `adj.r.squared.factor` | `0.0001` | Selection tolerance: the regression with the most points whose adjusted R² is within this value of the best adjusted R² is chosen (favors more points when fits are nearly equal) |
| `r.squared.factor` | `NA` | The same tolerance on the unadjusted R² instead (≥ 0.13.0). Setting either factor takes the other out of use, so exactly one is in use; `NA` means "select on the other one" |
| `min.hl.r.squared` | `0.9` | Minimum unadjusted R² for λz acceptance (post-hoc exclusion via `exclude_nca_min.hl.r.squared()`) |
| `min.span.ratio` | `2` | Minimum ratio of time span to half-life (post-hoc exclusion via `exclude_nca_span.ratio()`) |
| `allow.tmax.in.half.life` | `FALSE` | Allow the Tmax timepoint in the λz regression |
| `hl_method` | `"log-linear"` | `"log-linear"` (OLS) or `"tobit"` (censored likelihood) (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `tobit_n_points_penalty` | `0` | Exponent in the Tobit window-selection criterion (residual × n^penalty); positive values favor shorter windows (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `tobit_optim_control` | `list()` | Control list forwarded to `stats::optim()` for Tobit optimization (≥ 0.13.0) |

Details: the [Half-Life chapter](halflife.qmd), [Half-Life Calculation](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v06-half-life-calculation.html), and [Half-life calculation with Tobit regression](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v06-half-life-calculation-tobit.html).

**AUCinf extrapolation**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `max.aucinf.pext` | `20` | Maximum percent of AUCinf that may be extrapolated for AUCinf to be considered valid (post-hoc exclusion via `exclude_nca_max.aucinf.pext()`) |

**Sparse sampling**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `sparse_lambda_z_se` | `"delta"` | How the standard error of a sparse `aucinf.obs` or `aumcinf.obs` accounts for the estimated λz: `"delta"` adds its uncertainty with the delta method; `"none"` treats λz as known (≥ 0.13.0). See the [Sparse Sampling chapter](sparse.qmd) |

**Concentration handling**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `conc.na` | `"drop"` | NA concentrations: `"drop"` removes them; a number substitutes that value |
| `conc.blq` | `list(first="keep", middle="drop", last="keep")` | BLQ concentrations: `"drop"`, `"keep"`, or a number globally; or a named list with keys `first` (before first non-BLQ), `middle` (between non-BLQs), `last` (after last non-BLQ), or `before.tmax`/`after.tmax` |

**Tmax / Tmin**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `first.tmax` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` = return first Tmax when tied; `FALSE` = return last |
| `first.tmin` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` = return first Tmin when tied; `FALSE` = return last (≥ 0.13.0) |

**Automatic intervals**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `auto.interval.method` | `"builder"` | Where the parameters of automatically generated intervals come from: `"builder"` asks `pknca_interval_table()` for the parameters and imputation that suit each interval; `"legacy"` uses the pre-0.13.0 lists (`single.dose.aucs` for a single dose; AUClast, Cmax, and Tmax for each dosing interval) (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `auto.interval.tolerance` | `0.05` | How far before an interval boundary a sample may be drawn and still count as the sample at that boundary, as a fraction of the interval length (a trough at 167.5 h still ends an interval nominally ending at 168 h) (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `single.dose.aucs` | (data frame) | Intervals for single-dose data, used only with `auto.interval.method = "legacy"` |
| `tau.choices` | `NA` | Candidate dosing intervals (τ) considered when detecting the dosing interval of multiple-dose data; `NA` considers any interval |

The [Automatic Intervals and Dosing Regimens chapter](auto-intervals.qmd) shows these options at work.

**Summary / output / other**

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `max.missing` | `0.5` | Maximum fraction of missing values allowed before suppressing a summary statistic |
| `keep_interval_cols` | `NULL` | Additional columns from the intervals data frame to carry through to results |
| `allow_partial_missing_units` | `FALSE` | Allow some parameters to lack unit definitions when a units table is provided |
| `progress` | `TRUE` | Show a progress bar during `pk.nca()` |
| `debug` | `NULL` | Enable internal debug output (not for routine use) |

Override for a single analysis by passing `options` to `PKNCAdata()`. To rerun with different settings, build a new `PKNCAdata` object with the new `options` and call `pk.nca()` again:

```{r}
o_data_strict <- PKNCAdata(
  o_conc, o_dose,
  options = list(
    min.hl.points  = 4,     # require at least 4 points for half-life
    min.hl.r.squared = 0.95 # stricter R² threshold
  )
)
```

`update()` has a method for `PKNCAresults` objects only (there is none for `PKNCAconc`, `PKNCAdose`, or `PKNCAdata`). `update(o_nca, data = o_data_new)` is meant for the case where only the concentration or dose data change, such as an interactive app that excludes a point: it recalculates the groups whose data changed and keeps the other results. Any other difference between the old and new `PKNCAdata` objects, including different `options`, makes it recalculate everything with a `pknca_warning_full_recalculation` warning, so for a change of settings, calling `pk.nca()` on the new object directly is the clearer choice.

---

## Extracting and plotting results

`as.data.frame()` returns one row per group per interval per parameter — a tidy shape ready for dplyr and ggplot2. More result-handling patterns: [Post-Processing](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v07-post-processing.html).

```{r}
results_df <- as.data.frame(o_nca)

# Filter to one parameter
auclast_df <- results_df |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "auclast")

ggplot(auclast_df, aes(x = Subject, y = PPORRES)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "AUClast by Subject", x = "Subject", y = "AUClast (h·mg/L)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
